about: The scripted AI lesson for p2-static (2026-11-15, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with one recall question, on current.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about static electricity, charge that stays in one place on an object: why your hair can stand on end after you pull off a jumper, why you sometimes get a tiny shock from a door handle, and what is happening inside the materials.

steps.question: First, one quick question from the electricity lessons. What is electric current?

options.text: The rate of flow of charge
The amount of charge stored in a battery
The heat given off by a wire

steps.right: Yes: current is the rate of flow of charge. This lesson is about charge that stays put, or jumps.

wrong.other: Not quite. Current is the rate of flow of charge.
wrong.stored: Not quite: current is the rate of flow of charge, how much charge passes a point each second.
wrong.heat: Not quite: current is the rate of flow of charge, how much charge passes a point each second.

idk.hint: Current is about how much charge passes a point each second. Which button says that?

steps.answerWhy: Current is the rate of flow of charge: how much charge passes a point each second.

steps.text: Now, this lesson. Everything is made of atoms. Each atom has a tiny centre, called the nucleus, which holds particles called protons.

Charge is a property of some tiny particles that makes them push or pull on each other. It comes in two types, positive and negative. Protons carry positive charge. Around the nucleus are much lighter particles, electrons, which carry negative charge.
An atom has the same number of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges cancel out. That is why most objects have no overall charge.
Rub a balloon on a wool jumper and some electrons are rubbed off one material and onto the other. The protons stay where they are, deep inside the atoms. Only electrons move.

steps.question: Predict: when the balloon is rubbed on the wool, electrons move from the wool onto the balloon. What charge does the balloon end up with?
steps.right: Yes: negative. The balloon has gained electrons, so it has more negative charge than positive.

wrong.other: Not quite. The balloon has gained electrons, so it is negative.
wrong.pos: Not quite: negative. Electrons carry negative charge, and the balloon has gained some, so it has more negative charge than positive.
wrong.none: Not quite: negative. The balloon has gained electrons, which carry negative charge, so its charges no longer cancel.

idk.hint: Electrons carry negative charge. The balloon has gained some. Which button fits?

steps.answerWhy: The balloon has gained electrons, which are negative, so it is negatively charged.

steps.question: And the wool has lost some electrons. What charge is the wool left with?
steps.right: Yes: positive. The wool lost some electrons, so its protons now outnumber its electrons.

wrong.other: Not quite. The wool lost electrons, so it is positive.
wrong.neg: Not quite: positive. The wool lost some negative electrons, so its positive protons now outnumber them.
wrong.none: Not quite: positive. The wool lost some electrons, so its charges no longer cancel: the protons outnumber the electrons.

idk.hint: The wool still has all its protons, but fewer electrons. Is there more positive or more negative charge?

steps.answerWhy: The wool lost electrons, so its protons outnumber its electrons: it is positive.

steps.text: The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses them is left with an equal positive charge: exactly as much positive charge as the other has negative.
Moving electrons from one material to another by rubbing them together is called charging by rubbing.

Charging by rubbing works with materials that do not let charge move through them, like plastic, rubber, wool and polythene. A material like that is called an insulator, and its charge stays where it is.
A material that lets charge move through it, like a metal, is called a conductor. Charge put on a conductor spreads through it, and can flow away, for example through your hand into the ground.

steps.question: An acetate rod, a kind of plastic, is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. Which is true?

options.text: The rod lost electrons to the cloth
The rod gained protons from the cloth
The rubbing made new positive charge

steps.right: Yes: it lost electrons to the cloth, which became negative. A positive object is one that has lost electrons.

wrong.other: Not quite. The rod lost electrons to the cloth.
wrong.protons: Not quite: protons stay inside the atoms and cannot be rubbed off. The rod became positive because it lost electrons to the cloth.
wrong.made: Not quite: rubbing does not make charge, it only moves electrons. The rod became positive because it lost electrons to the cloth.

idk.hint: Only electrons can be rubbed off. To end up positive, did the rod gain them or lose them?

steps.answerWhy: Only electrons move, so the rod became positive by losing electrons to the cloth.

steps.prompt: In one line: how does rubbing make a balloon negatively charged?
points: electrons are rubbed onto the balloon from the other material
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: electrons are rubbed onto the balloon from the other material; only electrons move, not protons.

keyPoints.heading: Same and different types of charge

steps.text: Charged objects push or pull on each other. Hang two charged rods near each other on threads, and they swing one way or the other.

steps.question: Predict: polythene gains electrons from a cloth, so two polythene rods rubbed with a cloth are both negative. Hung near each other, which way do they swing?
steps.right: Yes: apart. Two objects with the same type of charge push each other away.

wrong.other: Not quite. They swing apart: the same type of charge pushes apart.
wrong.together: Not quite: they swing apart. Both rods have the same type of charge, negative, and the same type of charge pushes apart.
wrong.none: Not quite: they swing apart. Charged objects push or pull each other, and two with the same type of charge push apart.

idk.hint: Both rods have the same type of charge. Do you think they push each other away, or pull together? Which button fits?

steps.answerWhy: Both rods are negative, and the same type of charge pushes apart, so they swing apart.

steps.text: Two objects with the same type of charge repel: they push each other apart. A push like that between charged objects is called repulsion.

steps.question: Predict: now a negative polythene rod is hung near a positive acetate rod. Which way do they swing?
steps.right: Yes: together. One is negative and one is positive, and different types of charge pull together.

wrong.other: Not quite. They swing together: different types of charge pull together.
wrong.apart: Not quite: they swing together. Their charges are different types, and different types pull together.
wrong.none: Not quite: they swing together. Charged objects push or pull each other, and different types of charge pull together.

idk.hint: One rod is negative and the other positive. Same type pushes apart; what do you think different types do?

steps.answerWhy: One rod is negative and one is positive, and different types of charge pull together.

steps.text: Two objects with different types of charge, one positive and one negative, attract: they pull together. A pull like that between charged objects is called attraction.

steps.question: After you pull off a jumper, your hair can stand on end, each hair pushing away from the others. What does that tell you about the charges on the hairs?

options.text: They all have the same type of charge
Some are positive and some negative

steps.right: Yes: the hairs push apart, and only the same type of charge does that. Every hair has gained or lost electrons in the same way, so they all have the same charge.

wrong.other: Not quite. The hairs push apart, so they all have the same type of charge.
wrong.opposite: Not quite: positive and negative hairs would pull together. The hairs push apart, so they all have the same type of charge.
wrong.magnet: Not quite: this is not magnetism. The hairs are charged, and because they push apart, they all have the same type of charge.

idk.hint: Same type of charge pushes apart; different types pull together. The hairs push apart. Which button fits?

steps.answerWhy: The hairs push apart, and only the same type of charge does that.

steps.text: The objects do not need to touch: attraction and repulsion between charged objects are non-contact forces. A force is a push or a pull.
The closer two charged objects are, the stronger the force between them.

steps.question: A girl touches a negatively charged metal dome. She stands on a plastic mat, so charge cannot flow away to the ground. Metal and her body are conductors, so some charge spreads onto her, and her hair stands on end. Which is true?

options.text: She becomes negative, like the dome, and her hairs repel
She becomes positive, the opposite of the dome
Protons move from the dome onto her

steps.right: Yes: electrons spread from the dome onto her, so she becomes negative like the dome, and her negative hairs repel.

wrong.other: Not quite. Electrons spread onto her, so she becomes negative like the dome, and her hairs repel.
wrong.opposite: Not quite: electrons from the dome spread onto her, so she becomes negative, the same as the dome. Her hairs, all negative, repel.
wrong.protons: Not quite: protons stay inside the atoms. Electrons spread from the dome onto her, so she becomes negative and her hairs repel.

idk.hint: Electrons are negative, and they spread from the dome onto her. Which button says she becomes negative?

steps.answerWhy: Electrons spread from the dome onto her, so she becomes negative like the dome, and her negative hairs repel.

steps.prompt: In one line: when do two charged objects attract, and when do they repel?
points: the same type of charge repels
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: two objects with the same type of charge repel, and two with different types attract.

steps.text: Here is how a charged object can push or pull something it is not touching. A charged object has an electric field around it: the region where another charged object feels a force.
The field is strongest close to the charged object. The further away you go, the weaker the field, and the weaker the force on another charged object.
Field lines are drawn to show an electric field. Each line has an arrow on it, showing the way the force would act on a small positive charge put there.

Look at the picture. Around a single charged sphere, the field lines are straight and meet its surface at right angles, like the spokes of a wheel. Around the positive sphere they point outwards; around the negative one, inwards.

steps.question: A small positive charge is put near the negative sphere in the picture. Which way does the force on it act?

options.text: Towards the sphere, along a field line
Round the sphere in a circle

steps.right: Yes: towards the sphere. The arrows point inwards, and a negative sphere pulls a positive charge in.

wrong.other: Not quite. The force is towards the sphere, along a field line.
wrong.away: Not quite: the arrows show the push on a small positive charge, and around the negative sphere they point inwards. So the force is towards the sphere.
wrong.circle: Not quite: the force acts along a field line. Around the negative sphere the lines point inwards, so the force is towards the sphere.

idk.hint: The arrows show which way a small positive charge is pushed. Around the negative sphere, which way do they point?

steps.answerWhy: The arrows around the negative sphere point inwards, so the force on a small positive charge is towards the sphere.

steps.text: Where the field lines are closer together, the field is stronger. Near each sphere the lines bunch up, so the field is strongest there, and they spread out further away, where it is weaker.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is an electric field, and how does it change as you move away from the charged object?
points: the region where another charged object feels a force
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force, and it gets weaker further away.

steps.text: Near a very highly charged object, the electric field is very strong. If it is strong enough, the air nearby starts to let charge through, and electrons jump across the gap to or from a nearby object. A jump like that is called a spark.

You may have felt one. Walking across some carpets rubs electrons onto you or off you, so you become charged. When your hand gets close to a metal door handle, electrons jump between you and the handle: a tiny spark, and a small shock.
Lightning is the same thing on a huge scale: so much charge builds up in a storm cloud that a giant spark jumps between the cloud and the ground.

steps.question: A highly charged object is moved closer to a metal pole. Which is true?
steps.right: Yes: closer means a stronger field, so a spark is more likely.

wrong.other: Not quite. The field is stronger closer to the object, so a spark is more likely.
wrong.less: Not quite: the field is stronger closer to a charged object, so a spark is more likely.
wrong.same: Not quite: the field is stronger closer to a charged object, so a spark is more likely when it is closer.

idk.hint: The electric field is strongest close to a charged object. Does a stronger field make a spark more or less likely?

steps.answerWhy: The field is stronger closer to a charged object, so a spark is more likely.

steps.text: Sparks can be dangerous. Even a small spark near petrol vapour or another flammable gas can start a fire or an explosion.

steps.prompt: In one line: what causes a spark?
points: a very strong electric field near a charged object
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: near a highly charged object the electric field is very strong, so electrons jump through the air.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz on the whole lesson: seven questions. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 7: Which particles move when two insulators are rubbed together?

wrong.w1: Not quite. Protons stay inside the atoms. Only electrons move.
wrong.w2: Not quite. The atoms stay where they are. Only electrons move.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 7: A cloth loses electrons to a rod. What charge is the cloth left with?
steps.right: Yes. Losing electrons leaves it positive.

wrong.other: Not quite. The cloth is positive.
wrong.w1: Not quite. Losing negative electrons leaves the cloth positive.
wrong.w2: Not quite. The cloth lost electrons, so it is positive.

steps.answerWhy: Losing electrons leaves the cloth positive.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 7: Two positively charged balloons are held close together. Which is true?
steps.right: Yes. The same type of charge repels.

wrong.w1: Not quite. The same type of charge repels.
wrong.w2: Not quite. Charged objects exert forces on each other: the same type repels.

steps.answerWhy: The same type of charge repels.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 7: Which way do the field lines around a positively charged sphere point?
steps.right: Yes. Outwards, the way a small positive charge would be pushed.

wrong.w1: Not quite. Inwards is for a negative sphere. Around a positive one they point outwards.
wrong.w2: Not quite. The field lines are straight, pointing outwards from a positive sphere.

steps.answerWhy: Around a positive sphere, the field lines point outwards.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 7: Further away from a charged object, which is true about its electric field?
steps.right: Yes. The field gets weaker further away.

wrong.other: Not quite. It is weaker further away.
wrong.w1: Not quite. The field is strongest close to the object and weaker further away.
wrong.w2: Not quite. The field gets weaker further away.

steps.answerWhy: The field gets weaker further from the charged object.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 7: What is an electric field?

options.text: The region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force
The charge stored on a charged object
The region around a magnet where iron feels a force

steps.right: Yes. The region where another charged object feels a force.

wrong.other: Not quite. It is the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force.
wrong.w1: Not quite. The field is not the charge itself. It is the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force.
wrong.w2: Not quite. A region round a magnet is a magnetic field. An electric field is the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force.

steps.answerWhy: An electric field is the region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force.

steps.question: Quiz, question 7 of 7: Do two charged objects need to touch to push or pull on each other?

options.text: No: it is a non-contact force

steps.right: Right: they do not need to touch. It is a non-contact force: each object is in the other's electric field, so it feels a force.

wrong.other: Not quite. It is a non-contact force.
wrong.w1: Not quite. Attraction and repulsion between charges are non-contact forces. A force is a push or a pull.

steps.answerWhy: Attraction and repulsion between charges are non-contact forces. A force is a push or a pull.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
